content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors utilized conditional value at risk to propose a robust version of proximal policy optimization method.  The authors demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method empirically through a detailed experimental comparison.
content.main_review:
Strengths
- The paper is well-written, especially the part of introducing the related method such as cvar and the new proposed method, which are both very easy to follow.
- In Sec.4, the authors explains clearly why the proposed method might be robust to adversarial disturbance based on the presented Theorem 3 and Theorem 4.
- The authors conduct detailed experiments to validate the proposed method, under different attacking settings. 

Weakness
- For the compared baselines, I feel the authors should add two additional baselines which are quite related to your introduction part of Section 2, the first one is mean + variance penalty method, which I think is a naive baseline. Another baseline I think is to select top performance trajectories according to a relatively portion (which I think is also quite related). I do not expect these two methods to work in your experiments, but I think it is really good to add these two. 

- When the authors introduce Theorem 1, I feel it is better to define the cost function, rather than reward function (thus you need to deal with $-D(\pi)$), and by defining cost function, it is also convenient to connect the current method with previous methods, and I think it is worth a clarification and comparison with a line of methods proposed by Yinlam Chow.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall I recommend an acceptance of the paper, while the authors may add some additional baselines, with some discussion to distinguish the current work with previous ones to address the concerns. 


-------------------

Thank the authors for the detailed response. I have read the authors response and also other reviewers's comments.  I feel the authors should modify the paper according to the suggestions and submit to another conference.

- Would the authors clarify the exact difference of using reward to derive the cvar approach rather than cost? Still I don't get why there are difference, the only thing you need is to change the sign of the cost function.

- The theorem in section 4, I feel they are less related to the cvar policy you propose. The authors argue that the core contribution of this work is to propose the connection between observation disturbance and transition disturbance. if so, I feel the authors should clarify more, otherwise to me what your core contribution is proposing cvar policy, rather than the theorems you just talk about (The structure of the paper may need to reorganize if you want to argue the core contribution).

- Still, the authors may add some more related baselines to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose an RL method to improve the average reward while guaranteeing (some kind of) worst-case return that is evaluated by CVaR. They also provide a theoretical analysis of how optimizing policies using CVaR can improve the robustness of the policies.
content.main_review:
strengths:  
+ The authors make both theoretical analyses (Sections 3 and 4) and empirical experiments (Section 5) to demonstrate the advantage of utilizing CVaR for safe RL. In particular, the analysis (which introduced the concept of VFR) and its results in Section 4 are new and meaningful in demonstrating the usefulness of CVaR.

weaknesses:

- The novelty of the methodological framework and the experiments is somewhat insufficient. 
  - The methodological framework: 
    - There is little improvement from that proposed in Chow et al.'s paper [1]: 
      - In Section 2.2, the authors point out the problem with Chow et al.'s method [1] as "However, these works ignore the reward in MDP and thus cannot be directly used in RL settings." But, this is misleading because, if we regard the reward and return multiplied by a negative coefficient (e.g., -1) as the cost and loss, respectively, then we can use reward in Chow et al's method. (As another approach, we can use reward in their method by calculating CVaR for the lower tail instead of the upper tail of the return distribution.) (Actually, in the paper under review, the authors utilize Chow et al's method by doing so.)
      - The discussion in Section 3 is essentially identical to the discussion in Chow et al.'s paper [1]. For example, it has already been proven in [1] (more precisely, in [2]) that Eq. 9 can be converted into Eq. 10. Also, the Lagrangian relaxation of the objective and derivation of gradients to optimize it (Eqs. 11~14) has already been done in [1].  
  - Experiments (Section 5). 
    - In  Hiraoka et al. [3], the PPO variant that optimizes Eq. 11 has already been proposed and evaluated in MuJoCo environments (e.g., Hopper and Halfcheetah) where the value of robot body masses are randomized (CPPO is basically identical to Hiraoka et al's PPO variant that uses a single option).  So, it is not clear if the findings provided in Section 5 make significant progress from the one provided in [3]. 

[1] Yinlam Chow and Mohammad Ghavamzadeh. Algorithms for cvar optimization in MDPs. NeurIPS, 2014  
[2] R. Rockafellar and S. Uryasev. Optimization of conditional value-at-risk. Journal of Risk, 26:1443–1471,
2002  
[3] Takuya Hiraoka, Takahisa Imagawa, Tatsuya Mori, Takashi Onishi, Yoshimasa Tsuruoka. Learning Robust Options by Conditional Value at Risk Optimization. NeurIPS, 2019. 


Minor comments:  
- It is better to compare with more studies that introduce CVaR into RL. 
Indeed, Chow et al.'s studies are seminal on CVaR x RL, but there are many other studies (e.g., [4--7]). 

[4] Morimura, T., Sugiyama, M., Kashima, H., Hachiya, H., and Tanaka, T. Nonparametric return
distribution approximation for reinforcement learning. ICML, 2010  
[5] Rajeswaran, A., Ghotra, S., Levine, S., and Ravindran, B. EPOpt: Learning Robust Neural
Network Policies Using Model Ensembles. ICLR, 2017  
[6] Elita A. Lobo, Mohammad Ghavamzadeh, Marek Petrik, Soft-Robust Algorithms for Batch Reinforcement Learning, https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.14495.  
[7] Will Dabney, Georg Ostrovski, David Silver, Rémi Munos, Implicit Quantile Networks for Distributional Reinforcement Learning, ICML 2018.  

- Theoretical Analysis
  - Optimizing Eq. 9 is not exactly the same as optimizing Eq. 15. 
So, if possible, it would be more convincing if you add theoretical (or experimental) evidence to support the following statement in Section 4.3: "Moreover, our CVaR-based optimization objective (9) focuses ....  observation disturbance as well as transition disturbance."  
  - Does the RL methods that optimize Eq. 2 also tend to reduce $ \hat{V}_{\mathcal{M}, \pi} $? The methods maximize the worst-case return (i.e., produce conservative policy), and thus $\max V$ could be close to $\min V$. 

- Typos?:  
Policy Proximal Optimization (PPO) -> Proximal Policy Optimization  
and use CVaR to evaluate. -> and use CVaR to evaluate it. ?  
Algorithms for cvar optimization in mdps. -> Algorithms for CVaR optimization in MDPs.
content.summary_of_the_review: I am leaning toward recommending rejection. The theoretical analysis made in Section 4 is novel and meaningful, but I could not find the significant novelty in the other part of the paper.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable review
content.comment:
We would like to address some of your concerns.

**Q1:** The novelty of the methodological framework

**A1:** Thanks a lot for your advice. Our methodological framework follows the previous framework proposed in previous work (Chow 2017) with some modifications to better fit the standard RL setting. For example, the previous framework (Chow 2017) considers risk-MDP with risk signals as return but there is always reward signals in the standard RL setting, thus we propose our methodological framework to regard the risk as a smoothing decreasing function of the reward (we use opposite sign as a special case in the paper and we will talk about a more general situation in the revised version). Actually, although CPPO includes some improvements from previous work for better fitting the standard RL setting, it is not the core contribution of this work and our main contribution is the theoretical analysis (sec 4). In sec 4, we first theoretically prove that though observation disturbance and transition disturbance are structurally different, their impact on performance decline is both based on VFR. Moreover, we further propose CVaR-based constraint can help to find more robust policies and we will explain it more clearly in the revised version.

**Q2:** The novelty of the experiments

**A2:** Thanks a lot for your reference. The pseudo-code of CPPO is just the core part of our algorithm and there are some modifications in practice. For example, we find it is inefficient to fix $\beta$ since the performance of the policy will increase during the training stage and we will gradually increase $\beta$ in the training stage. We will provide a more detailed pseudo code in the revised version. Moreover, our experiments also evaluate the performance of algorithms under observation disturbance and transition disturbance and further indicate the effectiveness of our theoretical analysis (Theorem 3 and Theorem 4). 

**Q3:** Theoretical analysis

**A3:** Thank you for your advice. We will state the connection between the theorems in sec 4 and CVaR-based RL more clearly in the revised version. Actually, our theoretical analysis (Theorem 3 and Theorem 4) indicates that the impact on performance under observation disturbance as well as transition disturbance will depend on VFR, which is the difference between the value function of the best state and the worst state, i.e. $\max_s V_{\mathcal{M}, \pi}(s)-\min_s V_{\mathcal{M}, \pi}(s)$. Since we need to control $\hat{V}_{\mathcal{M}, \pi}$ for a more robust policy, it's more reasonable to improve the performance of the worst state rather than to reduce the performance of the best state. Thus our theoretical result provides a better understanding of the robustness of existing conservative methods (e.g. control the value of the worst case). However, as mentioned in sec 2.1, it's intractable to optimize these max-min problems and these conservative methods may receive extremely conservative policies. Thus we point out that CVaR-optimized RL can loosen the objective and find a trade-off in sec 3.1. 

**Q4:** Some typos

**A4:** Thanks a lot for your kind suggestions, we will correct them in the revised version.

Ref:

Yinlam Chow et al. Risk-constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria. The Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR), 18(1):6070–6120, 2017

But, I think the discussion in the rest part of Section 3 (except for the algorithm design part (the last paragraph of Section 3.1)) can also be extensible to the general case.  

However, is it really necessary to extend the discussion to the general case? 
I think providing examples of RL tasks that the special case (using $-D(\tau)$) can not cover (i.e., motivating examples) would make it clear. 



> *Actually, although CPPO includes some improvements from previous work for better fitting the standard RL setting, it is not the core contribution of this work and our main contribution is the theoretical analysis (sec 4). In sec 4, we first theoretically prove that though observation disturbance and transition disturbance are structurally different, their impact on performance decline is both based on VFR* 

> *We will state the connection between the theorems in sec 4 and CVaR-based RL more clearly in the revised version. Actually, our theoretical analysis (Theorem 3 and Theorem 4) indicates that the impact on performance..*  

> *Thus our theoretical result provides a better understanding of the robustness of existing conservative methods (e.g. control the value of the worst case). However, as mentioned in sec 2.1, it's intractable to optimize these max-min problems and these conservative methods may receive extremely conservative policies. Thus we point out that CVaR-optimized RL can loosen the objective and find a trade-off in sec 3.1.*  

In the revised version, the connection between CVaR-based RL methods and the discussion in Section 4 is more clearly explained.  

However, the discussion in Section 4 does not provide sufficient theoretical support that CVaR-based RL methods are more useful than other robust RL methods (in certain settings, e.g., observation/transition disturbance settings).  
I understand your justifications:  
"However, as mentioned in Sec 3.1, directly maximizing the value function of the worst state may cause our policy to be over conservative."  
and  
"As mentioned in Sec 2.1, some safe RL objectives, such as problems (2) and (3), are intractable max-min problems."  
But, these justifications come from a practical viewpoint, not from a theoretical viewpoint. 
(Theorems 3 and 4 themselves do not imply that CVaR-based methods are better than other robust RL methods.)   

Providing additional theoretical support for this would make your work much stronger. 
(The analyses in Section 4 in the current version is beneficial at the point that it clarifies the nature of CVaR-based and other RL methods, and can be left in the paper.)



Minor comments:  
I'm not sure whether an analysis method that uses the TV-distance to derive inequalities, as in the one for Theorems 3 and 4, is appropriate to argue for the usefulness of CVaR-based RL methods compared to other (especially robust) RL methods.  
This type of analysis method assumes a kind of worst-case ($ \max_{s} ... $) when bounding the performance residuals, which would make the resulting inequality unnecessarily pessimistic for CVaR-based RL methods.  
Perhaps, it would be interesting to make additional analyses about how the distribution of the performance residuals differs between CVaR-based and other robust RL methods.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focus on the conditional value-at-risk of the return as a measure of the `safety' of a policy. The CVaR-PPO algorithm is developed to learn a policy which maximizes return while satisfying a certain value of the CVaR. Theorems are developed to relate the safety of policies under adversarial state and observation perturbations and various MDP quantities. Finally, empirical results show that the proposed CVaR-PPO leads to higher reward and more robust policies.
content.main_review:
This paper argues for the relevance of the conditional value-at-risk of the return as an important quantity for robust reinforcement learning. 
An algorithm is presented for learning a policy which is reward-maximizing, subject to being $\alpha, \beta$-CVaR. Put simply, this means that when looking at the distribution of the return, the average of the worst-$\alpha$-fraction of the return is greater than $\beta$. The authors do a good job of arguing that this measure of risk is often easier to specify for the practitioner as a natural metric for risk. However, it's unclear to me how novel the work is, as the authors seem to miss some related work and downplay the similarity to other work. This needs to be addressed by the authors. Meanwhile, the experiments and theory section are nice, but could be tied back more to the overall goal of the importance of learning a CVaR policy.

Comments and questions for the authors:

1. At the bottom of page 4, there is a lot of language suggesting that it's possible to find a solution to equation 9. However, it seems that there is no reason to expect that a solution always exists--if $\beta$ is greater than the maximum total return it seems like there is no way to satisfy equation 9. Is this correct?
2. Theorem 2 is interesting, but hard to understand without some more context. What are the implications of this result?
3. Can the authors comment on the similarity of their algorithm to 'Risk-Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Percentile Risk Criteria', which is (chow 2017) in the paper? It appears that the algorithm in equations 7-9 in Chow and 12-14 in this paper are very similar, perhaps identical. The authors say that they are different since the previous work examines the cost instead of reward, but as I understand it the 'cost' is simply reward with the opposite sign (hence $\beta$ and $\nu$ having opposite signs in the previous work). Flipping a sign does not make a substantially different algorithm, but it's possible I've misunderstood the connection between the two papers so would appreciate a comment.
4. The theorems in section 4 are nice, but the connection to the actual approach of CVaR-optimized RL is not clear. Unlike the precise results in section 4.2, section 4.3 is vague. Is there anything you can actually prove about how a ($\alpha,\beta$)-CVaR policy is robust to observation and transition perturbations? As it is, there is a suggestion that they would be, but no proof. Even a result in some restricted setting would be useful. As it is, the results in 4.2 do not seem very relevant to the rest of the paper without a stronger connection to the CVaR policies
5. Section 5 seems to be missing some key information and results. Firstly, there doesn't seem to be any mention of the values of ($\alpha, \beta$) used in the experiments. Secondly, there is no evaluation that the learned policies actually are $(\alpha, \beta)$-CVaR robust. I'd expect at least a table showing that the policies solve the problem which the paper deals with, i.e. that the algorithm works. Obviously there is a bit of a possible loophole if the ($\alpha, \beta$) values were chosen to be vacuously feasible. Thirdly, could the authors explain how it appears that CPPO outperforms regular PPO on the mean reward metric? I would have expected the training curves to look something like PPO achieving higher mean reward with a large variance, while CPPO achieves either the same or lower mean reward with a smaller variance (possibly with an asymmetric spread that is smaller on the lower side). As the authors point out (with oracle optimization etc) the CVaR-robust model obviously must have equal or worse mean return. Therefore there is something else going on with the Lagrangian procedure influencing the learning dynamics, or possibly some extra tricks used with the CVaR but not the PPO agent; it's hard to know without the code or more training details. 

Summarizing:

Strengths:
+ Convincing arguments about the importance of CVaR for RL
+ Nice theorems in section 4.

Weaknesses:
+ Potential lack of novelty due to similarity to previous work
+ Lack of connection in section 4,5 to the rest of the work
+ Missing some key information and needed evaluations in section 5
+ Some unclear language around existence of CVaR-feasible policies



Minor Points
In 5.2 CPPO is said to be labelled in pink but it is orange in the graph

Figure 3 would be easier to understand if they were labelled with respect to the ground-truth parameter, i.e. +1kg, -1kg from training mass etc.

After equation 10, 'deviation' should be 'derivation'


--------------------------------------------------------
Update 2021-11-21
Based on the authors' feedback I have raised my score to 5. The authors argue that the main contribution is the theoretical analysis. The theory is nice and a decent contribution. If the rest of the paper were up to the same standard as section 4, I would strongly recommend accepting. However, currently the other sections are not very well-motivated with connections to the theory (although the new thm 5 is an improvement in this regard). It seems like the novelty of the proposed algorithm is quite limited in view of previous work. Overall I think the paper is borderline, but a substantial revision addressing similarity to previous work and with a more comprehensive experiments section could be a very strong paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is a good advocate for the importance of CVaR in reinforcement learning. However the main algorithm has a striking similarity to previous work that is not really addressed in the paper. The experiments lack important details and don't show that the algorithm fulfills its stated aims.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable review (Part 1)
content.comment:
We would like to address some of your concerns.

**Q1:** About contributions and novelty

**A1:** Thanks for your question. We would emphasize that the main contributions and novelty of this work are that we find the connection between the observation disturbance and the transition disturbance by VFR (Theorem 3 and Theorem 4) and further propose that CVaR-based constraint can generate more robust policies under disturbance (we will provide some more detailed analysis in the revised version). To the best of our knowledge, the theoretical analysis of these two parts has not been proposed in previous works. Also, following the previous CVaR-based framework (Chow 2017), we modify it to fit the standard RL setting and propose our CPPO based on PPO. We will make it more clear in the final. 

**Q2:** About the bottom of page 4

**A2:** Thank you for your advice. The existence of the optimal policy $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$ is based on the constrained region. $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$ does not exist if the constrained region is an empty set, for example, when $\beta>\max_{\tau}D(\tau)$. However, at the bottom of page 4, we do not focus on whether $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$ exists and whether it's possible to find $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$. This part of the paper (the bottom of page 4 and the top of page 5) suppose that the constrained region is reasonable thus there exists $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$ and is aiming at analyzing the properties of $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$, including the probability of receiving bad return is under a certain value and the expected return of $\pi_c(\alpha,\beta)$ can be controlled by a lower bound(Theorem 2).

**Q3:** The implications of Theorem 2

**A3:** Thank you for your positive supportive review about Theorem 2. By Theorem 2, we provide a low bound of the performance of $\pi_{c}(\alpha,\beta)$ and point out that $\pi_{c}(\alpha,\beta)$ will not perform too bad although it is trained under certain constraints.

**Q4:** The similarity and connection of CPPO to previous work (Chow 2017)

**A4:** Thanks a lot for your advice. Our algorithm CPPO follows the framework proposed in previous work (Chow 2017) with some modifications to fit the standard RL setting. For example, previous work (Chow 2017) considers an MDP with risk signals but there is always reward signals rather than risk signals in the standard RL setting, thus we propose to regard the risk as a smoothing decreasing function of the reward (we use the opposite sign in the paper and we will talk about a more general situation in the revised version). Actually, although there are some improvements of the algorithm we use compared with previous work, it is not the core contribution of this work and our main contribution is the theoretical analysis of policies' robustness under disturbance. First, we theoretically prove that the performance degradation under observation disturbance and transition
disturbance depends on VFR. Furthermore, we theoretically propose that CVaR-based constraint can generate more robust policies under disturbance (we will provide some more detailed analysis in the revised version).

**Q5:** The connection between the theorems in Section 4 and the actual approach of CVaR-optimized RL

**A5:** We appreciate the kind suggestions and we will introduce the connection between the theorems in sec 4 and CVaR-based RL more clearly in the revised version. It seems that we have not stated the connection very clearly. Actually, our theoretical analysis (Theorem 3 and Theorem 4) indicates that the impact on performance under observation as well as transition will depend on VFR, which is the difference between the value function of the best state and the worst state, i.e. $ \max_s V_{\mathcal{M}, \pi}(s)-\min_s V_{\mathcal{M}, \pi}(s)$. Since we need to control $\hat{V}_{\mathcal{M}, \pi}$ for a more robust policy, it's more reasonable to improve the performance of the worst state rather than to reduce the performance of the best state. Thus our theoretical result provides a better understanding of the robustness of existing conservative methods (e.g. control the value of the worst case). However, as mentioned in sec 2.1, it's intractable to optimize these max-min problems and these conservative methods may receive extremely conservative policies. Thus we point out that CVaR-optimized RL can loosen the objective and find a trade-off in sec 3.1.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Built upon some previous work on CVaR-based RL,  this paper proposes a new policy optimization algorithm CPPO .   Theorems on performance degradation under observation disturbance and transition disturbance are provided.  Experimental results on MuJoCo are presented to demonstrate the advantage of the proposed method.
content.main_review:
On the positive side, the theorem statements in Section 4 are clean and interesting. It seems to me that this paper does make good contributions in the discounted MDP cases. However, I also do have some concerns regarding the significance of the results in this paper for continuous control applications. It seems that the authors are using MoJoCo to demonstrate CPPO and hence continuous control is their main target application. My main background is also from control, and there are a few things which are confusing to me.

1. The theorems in this paper seem to work on discounted cases. However, for many control tasks, it makes more sense to set the discount factor as 1 (e.g. Walker, etc). Do the theorems in this paper make sense for such control applications?  
2. I am looking at the proof for Theorem 4 (the model mismatch result). For continuous control problems, everything is in continuous space, does the proof still work? Simply just replacing sums with integrals? I am not sure whether that is the case or not.
3. The comparison with the exponential utility approach is also confusing. At least for control applications, it is well-known that exponential utility-based approach is equivalent to robust control in many situations and hence can induce robustness for control applications. For example, some classic and more recent references are given below.

[Glover1988] Glover, K. and Doyle, J. C. State-space formulae for all stabilizing controllers that satisfy an H∞-norm bound and relations to relations to risk sensitivity. Systems & Control Letters, 1988.

[Whittle1990] Whittle, P.  Risk-sensitive Optimal Control, 1990.

[Zhang2020] Zhang, K., Hu, B. and Basar, T. Policy Optimization for H2 Linear Control with H-Infinity Robustness Guarantee: Implicit Regularization and Global Convergence. L4DC, 2020.

It seems that this paper ignored the above connections between exponential utility and robust control. Some comments are needed to justify the proposed CPPO in the robust control context.
content.summary_of_the_review: I do think that the theory in this paper is interesting and relevant for discounted MDP problems. However, it seems that continuous control is the main target application for the proposed method, and there may be some gap between control practice and the results in this paper. Some clarifications are needed. Right now my score is 5. I am willing to increase my score if the authors can address my comments.

content.comment:
We would like to address some of your concerns.

**A1:** The discounted factor for control tasks

**Q1:** Thank you for your advice. Previous works always set $\gamma<1$ in continuous tasks like MuJoCo, i.e. the origin paper of PPO (Appendix A in Schulman 2017) and the implementation of PPO in SpinningUp (Achiam, J 2018) both set $\gamma=0.99$. Thus our theoretical consideration of discounted MDP is reasonable for continuous control tasks like MuJoCo. 


**A2:** Continuous situation in the proof

**Q2:** Thanks a lot for your careful reading of our proof. The writing style of our proof follows previous works (SA-MDP, Zhang H 2020). As you pointed out, we can replace sums with integrals to prove the continuous situations. We'd refine our proof to make it more clear for both discrete and continuous cases in the final version.

**A3:** The comparison with the exponential utility approach 

**Q3:** Thank you for your reference. We'll talk about these works about exponential utility in the final version. Because of the connection between exponential utility and variance, this work mainly considers that variance will penalize both the positive and negative risks, which may yield a drop of the agent's performance rather than infecting the robustness.
